content_config.text: 1. Overview — Why the Hip Behaves as It Does

content_config.body: The knee is unstable and mobile. The hip is the opposite: a deep, congruent ball-and-socket that is intrinsically stable and sacrifices some range to get there. It is also the joint that carries the highest loads in the body relative to its size. Almost everything characteristic about hip pathology follows from those two facts — deep containment and enormous load.

• The acetabulum is a true socket, enclosing rather more than half of the femoral head. Compare the glenoid, which contains barely a quarter of the humeral head.
  • The labrum deepens it further and creates a suction seal.
  • The capsule and its three ligaments are among the strongest in the body — the iliofemoral ligament is the strongest ligament in the human body.
  • Consequence: traumatic hip dislocation requires very high energy (a dashboard injury, a fall from height), unlike the shoulder. But when the hip does fail, it fails structurally — fracture, avascular necrosis, labral tear, arthritis — rather than through recurrent instability.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The clinical corollary of a deep socket: hip disease presents as stiffness and pain, not instability. When a patient does describe hip "giving way," it is far more often quadriceps inhibition, a labral tear catching, or referred pathology than true instability.

The exceptions worth knowing are dysplasia (a shallow socket) and generalised ligamentous laxity, in which genuine microinstability does occur.

rows: Reduced to ~90° with the knee extended — hamstring tension, not the joint, is the limit
Limited by the iliofemoral ligament, which is why we can stand with minimal muscle activity
The first motion lost in hip osteoarthritis and the most sensitive to test

content_config.body:
• Level walking: ~30° flexion, 10° extension, 5° each of abduction/adduction and rotation.
  • Stairs: ~65–70° flexion.
  • Sitting in a standard chair: ~90°. Rising from a low chair or toilet: up to ~110°.
  • Tying a shoelace, putting on socks, cutting toenails: ~110–120° flexion with rotation and adduction — the combination that is genuinely hard to substitute for.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Test internal rotation first in any patient with hip, groin or thigh pain. It is the earliest motion lost in osteoarthritis and in synovitis of any cause, because the capsule is tightest in that direction. Loss of internal rotation in flexion is one of the more useful physical signs in musculoskeletal medicine.

For function, the deficit that disables patients is not loss of extension (as at the knee) but loss of the flexion–adduction–rotation combination — reaching the foot. Ask specifically about socks, shoes and toenails; it is a better functional question than any range measurement.
1.3 Load — the lever arm that explains everything

content_config.body:
• In single-leg stance, the body weight acts at the midline, a long distance from the hip centre. The abductors act on the greater trochanter, a short distance from it.
  • The abductor lever arm is roughly one third the length of the body-weight lever arm. So the abductors must generate about twice body weight to hold the pelvis level.
  • Their force plus body weight passes through the joint, giving a hip joint reaction force of roughly 2.5–3 × body weight in single-leg stance.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
This single calculation is the basis of most conservative hip management.

A cane in the CONTRALATERAL hand works because it applies an upward force far from the hip on the opposite side, generating a large counter-moment. It reduces the joint reaction force by roughly a third, far more than the small weight actually taken through the arm. Putting the cane in the ipsilateral hand achieves almost nothing.

Weight loss is amplified — each kilogram lost removes roughly three to four kilograms of load from the hip during walking.

Carrying a load on the SAME side as the painful hip reduces the load (it shortens the effective body-weight moment arm); carrying it on the opposite side increases it. Counterintuitive, and worth telling patients.

Abductor strengthening reduces the compensatory lurch, but note that stronger abductors also generate higher joint reaction force — which is why in advanced arthritis, gait aids and load reduction often help more than strengthening alone.

content_config.body:
• Formed by all three pelvic bones: ilium (~2/5), ischium (~2/5) and pubis (~1/5), meeting at the triradiate cartilage, which fuses at about 14–16 years.
  • Lunate surface — the horseshoe-shaped articular cartilage, open inferiorly.
  • Acetabular fossa — the central non-articular depression, containing the pulvinar (fibrofatty tissue) and the ligamentum teres.
  • Acetabular notch — the inferior gap in the horseshoe, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament, which completes the ring and through which vessels enter.

content_config.text: 2.1.2 Orientation and the numbers that matter

rows: Retroversion causes anterior pincer impingement (crossover sign on radiograph)

content_config.body:
• The head is about two-thirds of a sphere, covered in cartilage except at the fovea capitis, where the ligamentum teres attaches.
  • Neck–shaft angle: 125–135° in adults. >140° = coxa valga; <120° = coxa vara.
  • Femoral anteversion: 10–20° in adults (30–40° at birth, decreasing through growth). Excess anteversion produces in-toeing, a preference for W-sitting in children, and increased internal rotation with reduced external rotation.
  • The neck exists to lateralise the femoral shaft, clearing the pelvis and giving the abductors a working lever arm. The price is a long cantilever carrying enormous bending load — which is why it fractures.

• Principal compressive trabeculae — from the medial cortex into the head, along the lines of compressive stress.
  • Principal tensile trabeculae — arcing from the lateral cortex across the neck into the inferior head.
  • Ward’s triangle — the relatively empty zone between the trabecular groups in the neck; a site of mechanical weakness and a region assessed in osteoporosis.
  • Calcar femorale — a dense vertical plate of bone from the posteromedial neck into the shaft. It is the main internal strut, and its integrity determines the stability of intertrochanteric fractures.

rows: Gluteus medius (the main abductor footprint; the site of gluteal tendinopathy)
Obturator internus with the gemelli; obturator externus

content_config.body:
• Anteriorly, the capsule attaches along the intertrochanteric line — so the whole anterior neck is intracapsular.
  • Posteriorly, it attaches about 1 cm proximal to the intertrochanteric crest — so the distal posterior neck is extracapsular.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
This line is the single most important prognostic division in hip fractures.

Intracapsular (subcapital, transcervical) fractures disrupt the retinacular vessels running along the neck, so they carry a high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union — hence arthroplasty in older or displaced cases.

Extracapsular (intertrochanteric, subtrochanteric) fractures occur in well-vascularised metaphyseal bone. AVN is rare and they are fixed rather than replaced.

When you read an operation note, the fracture location tells you the blood supply story, the AVN risk, and the rehabilitation trajectory before you read another word.

content_config.body:
• A fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the bony acetabular margin, continuous inferiorly with the transverse acetabular ligament. Triangular in cross-section.
  • It deepens the socket, increasing the articular surface area by about 20–25% and the acetabular volume by about 30%.
  • The suction seal is its most important function: the labrum seals the joint, maintaining negative intra-articular pressure and a pressurised layer of synovial fluid. This fluid film is what allows near-frictionless movement and distributes load across the cartilage.
  • Blood supply is peripheral only — the outer third, from the obturator and gluteal vessels. The inner portion and the labrochondral junction (a watershed zone) are avascular, which is why tears there do not heal.
  • It is richly innervated with nociceptors and mechanoreceptors — a genuine pain generator and a proprioceptive organ.
  • The anterosuperior labrum is the commonest site of tearing, because it is where impingement occurs and where the labrum is thinnest.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Losing the suction seal matters more than the tear itself. Once the seal fails, fluid is expressed from the joint under load, cartilage contact stress rises, and degeneration accelerates. This is the mechanism linking labral pathology to early osteoarthritis, and the rationale for repairing rather than excising the labrum.

Clinically: a labral tear typically causes groin pain with clicking, catching or giving way, worse in deep flexion, sitting, and pivoting. The FADIR test (flexion–adduction–internal rotation) is sensitive but not specific.

Be careful attributing symptoms to imaging: labral abnormalities appear on MRI in a large proportion of asymptomatic adults, rising steeply with age.

content_config.body:
• Attaches proximally to the acetabular rim, labrum and transverse acetabular ligament; distally as described in 2.2.4.
  • The zona orbicularis is a circular collar of deep capsular fibres encircling the femoral neck. It has no bony attachment and acts like a buttonhole, resisting distraction and helping hold the head in the socket.
  • Retinacular fibres (of Weitbrecht) run proximally along the neck beneath synovial reflections, carrying the vessels to the head — the anatomical reason a displaced neck fracture threatens the head’s blood supply.

rows: AIIS → intertrochanteric line, as two limbs forming an inverted Y
Extension and external rotation. The strongest ligament in the body (~350 N)
Internal rotation and extension. The weakest of the three

content_config.body: • All three spiral in the same direction, so all tighten in extension and wind the head firmly into the socket, and all relax in flexion.

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text:
"All three tighten in extension." That is why:

— you can stand for long periods with almost no hip muscle activity, hanging on the iliofemoral ligament;

— the close-packed position is extension with internal rotation and abduction;

— the position of comfort (loose-packed, maximum capsular volume) is about 30° flexion, 30° abduction and slight external rotation — exactly the posture a patient with a hip effusion or septic hip adopts;

— posterior dislocation occurs in flexion (the dashboard injury), when the ligaments are slack and the posterior capsule is unsupported.

content_config.body:
• The classic capsular pattern of the hip is restriction of internal rotation, then flexion, then abduction, with extension and external rotation relatively preserved early.
  • Internal rotation is lost first and most. A patient with groin pain and painless full internal rotation is unlikely to have significant intra-articular hip disease.

• Runs from the fovea capitis to the acetabular notch and transverse acetabular ligament.
  • Carries the artery of the ligamentum teres (from the obturator artery). This supplies a meaningful portion of the femoral head in young children, but only a small and variable amount in adults — it cannot compensate if the retinacular vessels are lost.
  • Its mechanical role is debated, but it is taut in flexion, adduction and external rotation and probably acts as a secondary stabiliser in deep flexion. It is also richly innervated and is increasingly recognised as a source of pain in its own right.
Twenty-odd muscles cross the hip. Learn them by function, not by compartment — that is how they present clinically and how they are rehabilitated.

rows: Psoas major: T12–L5 vertebral bodies and transverse processes. Iliacus: iliac fossa. Both → lesser trochanter
Psoas: ventral rami L1–L3 directly. Iliacus: femoral nerve (L2–L4)
The prime hip flexor. Psoas crosses the lumbar spine, so it is also a lumbar stabiliser. Its separate innervation is diagnostically useful
AIIS (straight head) + superior acetabular rim (reflected head) → patella
The only two-joint quadriceps — flexes hip and extends knee
Flexes, abducts and externally rotates — the "tailor’s" position
Iliac crest behind ASIS → iliotibial band → Gerdy’s tubercle
Flexes, abducts and internally rotates. Frequently overactive when gluteus medius is weak
Pectineal line of pubis → pectineal line of femur
Flexes and adducts; a common site of groin strain

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The psoas is innervated directly from the lumbar plexus roots (L1–L3), while the iliacus is supplied by the femoral nerve. This has two consequences worth knowing:

Hip flexion may be relatively preserved in a femoral nerve lesion, because psoas is spared — so weak knee extension with preserved hip flexion points to the femoral nerve, whereas both weak points higher, to the plexus or the L2–L4 roots.

A psoas haematoma or abscess (retroperitoneal, and classically in anticoagulated patients) can compress the femoral nerve within the iliacus compartment. The presentation is a painful hip held in flexion, with quadriceps weakness and anteromedial thigh numbness — a diagnosis it is easy to miss and important not to.

rows: Posterior ilium, sacrum, coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament → iliotibial band (~75%) and gluteal tuberosity (~25%)
The most powerful extensor, but recruited mainly for power tasks — stairs, rising from a chair, running. Barely active in level walking. Also a strong external rotator
The workhorse extensors in level gait; two-joint muscles
A powerful extensor; the only adductor with sciatic innervation

content_config.text: 4.3 Abductors — the group that matters most in PM&R

cells: Outer surface of the ilium, between the posterior and anterior gluteal lines

The principal hip abductor. Its anterior fibres internally rotate and its posterior fibres externally rotate, so it also controls femoral rotation. Critically, in single-leg stance it stabilises the pelvis in the frontal plane

Weakness produces the Trendelenburg sign. Its trochanteric insertion is the site of gluteal tendinopathy, the true cause of most "trochanteric bursitis". It is injured or denervated by the direct lateral surgical approach to the hip and by superior gluteal nerve traction
Outer ilium, between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines
Anterior facet of the greater trochanter, with a capsular expansion
Abduction and internal rotation; tensions the hip capsule during motion, acting as a dynamic capsular stabiliser

Often torn together with gluteus medius. Its capsular attachment means it has a proprioceptive as well as a mechanical role, which is one argument for targeted abductor retraining rather than generic strengthening

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The Trendelenburg sign, explained properly. Standing on the affected leg, the contralateral pelvis drops, because the weak abductors on the stance side cannot hold it level. The sign is named for the side that is weak, not the side that drops.

Compensated Trendelenburg (Duchenne lurch): rather than let the pelvis drop, the patient leans the trunk over the weak side. This moves the centre of mass toward the hip, shortening the body-weight lever arm and reducing the abductor force required. It looks like a lurch and is often mistaken for pain avoidance — it is mechanics.

Causes to work through: superior gluteal nerve injury (including iatrogenic), L5 radiculopathy, gluteal tendon tear or tendinopathy, hip osteoarthritis with pain inhibition, coxa vara or a prosthesis that has shortened the abductor lever arm, and simple deconditioning.

rows: The commonest site of groin strain in athletes; its tendinous origin at the pubis is easily palpated
The anterior division of the obturator nerve passes in front of it, the posterior division behind — a surgical landmark
The largest. The adductor hiatus transmits the femoral vessels into the popliteal fossa
The only two-joint adductor; also flexes the knee. A common graft donor

content_config.body: Six small muscles running roughly horizontally from the pelvis to the greater trochanter. They are the rotator cuff of the hip — short, deep, and functioning largely as dynamic stabilisers that compress the head into the socket.

rows: Passes through the greater sciatic foramen — the key landmark dividing it into supra- and infrapiriform portions. Becomes an abductor beyond ~60–90° of hip flexion
Exits the lesser sciatic foramen, turning sharply around the ischium
The only one supplied by the obturator nerve. Its tendon protects the medial femoral circumflex artery
Its nerve also supplies the hip joint. Ischiofemoral impingement occurs in the space between the ischium and lesser trochanter where it lies

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text:
Superior to inferior: Piriformis, Gemellus superior, Obturator internus, Gemellus inferior, Obturator externus, Quadratus femoris — "P-GO-GO-Q".

And a caution: the two obturators do not share a nerve. Obturator internus is supplied by its own sacral-plexus nerve; obturator externus by the obturator nerve.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
The sciatic nerve–piriformis relationship varies. In roughly 85% of people the undivided sciatic nerve passes below piriformis (Beaton type A). In the remainder the nerve is split by the muscle, passes through it, or runs above it.

This anatomical variation is often invoked to explain piriformis syndrome, but the modern and more useful framing is deep gluteal syndrome — sciatic entrapment anywhere in the subgluteal space, by piriformis, fibrous bands, the obturator internus–gemellus complex, or the hamstring origin.

It remains a diagnosis of exclusion: rule out lumbar radiculopathy first, since the two present almost identically and radiculopathy is far commoner.
5.1 Blood supply of the femoral head

content_config.body: The highest-yield vascular anatomy in the lower limb, because it determines who develops avascular necrosis.

rows: The dominant supply. From the profunda femoris (occasionally the femoral). Its deep branch runs posteriorly, gives off the posterosuperior retinacular vessels (lateral epiphyseal arteries), which pierce the capsule and run proximally along the femoral neck beneath the synovial retinacula to enter the head
Supplies the anterior and inferior portions of the head; a smaller and more variable contribution
From the obturator artery. Significant in children; small and variable in adults

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Two anatomical facts explain almost all femoral head AVN:

1. The retinacular vessels run along the neck, not through it. A displaced intracapsular neck fracture shears them directly, and a tense haemarthrosis within the intact capsule can tamponade them. Hence AVN rates of roughly 10–15% in undisplaced and up to 30–40% in displaced intracapsular fractures — and the rationale for arthroplasty rather than fixation in older patients.

2. The MFCA passes between quadratus femoris and obturator externus. The obturator externus tendon protects it, which is why the surgical dislocation approach preserves that tendon meticulously. It is also why posterior hip dislocation threatens the vessel and why urgent reduction matters — AVN risk rises steeply after about 6–12 hours.

Other causes follow the same final pathway: corticosteroids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, and (in children) Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease.

rows: Fascia lata, pierced by the saphenous opening

content_config.body:
• Contents, lateral to medial: N–A–V–E–L — femoral Nerve, femoral Artery, femoral Vein, Empty space (femoral canal), Lymphatics.
  • Note that the femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath, deep to the iliacus fascia — which is the anatomical basis of the fascia iliaca block, widely used for hip fracture analgesia.

rows: Injured by psoas haematoma, retractors, hip and pelvic surgery. Patellar reflex L3–L4
Compressed in pelvic surgery and obstetric injury. Its articular branch is why hip pathology refers to the knee
Injured in posterior hip dislocation (the peroneal division most), posterior surgical approach, and deep gluteal syndrome
Exits above piriformis. Injury → Trendelenburg gait. At risk in the direct lateral approach
Exits below piriformis. Injury → difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs
Passes under or through the inguinal ligament ~1 cm medial to the ASIS → meralgia paraesthetica
Also supplies the hip joint — an articular nerve

content_config.label: EMG / electrodiagnostics
content_config.text:
Localising a Trendelenburg gait. Weak abductors can come from the superior gluteal nerve, the L5 root, or the muscle itself.

Superior gluteal nerve lesion: gluteus medius, minimus and TFL abnormal; gluteus maximus normal (inferior gluteal), tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior normal.

L5 radiculopathy: gluteus medius abnormal plus tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior and often the paraspinals.

The discriminating muscles are therefore tibialis posterior and the lumbar paraspinals — both spared in a superior gluteal lesion.

Meralgia paraesthetica is purely sensory. If a patient with anterolateral thigh numbness has any quadriceps weakness or a reduced patellar reflex, the lesion is not the LFCN — think femoral nerve or the L2–L4 roots.

content_config.body: • Applying Hilton’s law, the hip is supplied by the nerves of the muscles crossing it:

rows: Femoral nerve (via branches to iliacus and rectus femoris) and the accessory obturator nerve when present
Nerve to quadratus femoris, and branches of the sciatic nerve

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
This table explains the most important referral pattern in the lower limb: hip pathology refers to the KNEE. The obturator nerve (L3) supplies both the hip joint and the skin over the medial and distal thigh, so hip disease is felt at the knee.

A child or adolescent presenting with knee pain and a normal knee examination must have the hip examined. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis and Legg–Calvé–Perthes disease classically present this way, and missing them causes permanent deformity.

The same principle applies in adults: hip osteoarthritis commonly presents as groin and anterior thigh pain radiating to the knee. Lateral hip pain is usually not the joint — it is far more often gluteal tendinopathy. Buttock pain is more often lumbar spine or sacroiliac.

The multi-nerve supply is also the basis of hip articular branch blocks and radiofrequency ablation (targeting the femoral and obturator articular branches) for patients unfit for arthroplasty — though the evidence base remains thinner than for genicular procedures at the knee.

rows: Between gluteus maximus / ITB and the posterolateral greater trochanter. The largest
The bursa traditionally blamed for "trochanteric bursitis"
Deep to the gluteus medius tendon, above the lateral facet
Deep to the gluteus minimus tendon, at the anterior facet
Between the iliopsoas tendon and the iliopectineal eminence. The largest bursa in the body; communicates with the joint in ~15%
Internal snapping hip; iliopsoas tendinopathy; can enlarge enormously in inflammatory arthritis and compress the femoral vessels or nerve
Between the ischial tuberosity and gluteus maximus
"Weaver’s bottom" — pain on prolonged sitting; overlaps with proximal hamstring tendinopathy

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
"Trochanteric bursitis" is usually the wrong diagnosis. Imaging and surgical series show that the dominant pathology in lateral hip pain is gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy or tearing, with bursal inflammation a secondary and often absent finding. The preferred term is greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS).

This is not pedantry — it changes treatment. A tendinopathy responds to progressive load, not to repeated corticosteroid injection, which gives short-term relief and worse outcomes at one year.

The anatomical key to management is compression. The gluteal tendons are compressed against the trochanter by the overlying ITB whenever the hip adducts. So the interventions that work are the ones that remove compression: avoid crossing the legs, avoid "hanging on one hip" when standing, avoid side-lying on the painful side (or place a pillow between the knees), and avoid aggressive ITB stretching and hip-adduction stretches, which increase compression rather than relieving it.

content_config.body:
• Clinical picture: lateral hip pain, tender directly over the greater trochanter, worse lying on that side at night, worse on stairs and prolonged standing.
  • Useful tests: single-leg stance for 30 seconds, the FABER test, and resisted hip abduction in side-lying. A positive Trendelenburg suggests a substantial tear.
  • Ultrasound distinguishes tendinopathy from a partial or full-thickness tear, which matters because full-thickness tears in an older patient may warrant surgical referral.

rows: Iliotibial band / gluteus maximus snapping over the greater trochanter
Lateral. Often visible and reproducible on request
Iliopsoas tendon snapping over the iliopectineal eminence or femoral head
Deep anterior groin; audible clunk on moving from flexion–abduction–external rotation to extension
Labral tear, loose body, chondral flap
Groin; associated with catching and giving way rather than a rhythmic snap

content_config.body:
• Iliac crest and ASIS — assess pelvic level and leg-length; the LFCN emerges just medial to the ASIS.
  • Greater trochanter — palpate the posterolateral aspect for the bursa and the lateral and anterior facets for the gluteal tendon insertions.
  • Ischial tuberosity with the hip flexed — hamstring origin and ischiogluteal bursa.
  • Pubic tubercle and adductor longus origin — the commonest site of groin strain.
  • Femoral triangle — femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point; the nerve lies lateral to it.
  • Anterior joint line — deep, ~2–3 cm lateral to the femoral pulse; too deep to palpate directly, but tenderness here supports intra-articular pathology.
  • Sacroiliac joints and lumbar spine — always, because they are the main sources of referred buttock pain.

content_config.text: 7.1.1 Provocative tests and what they actually test

content_config.body:
• FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) — anterior impingement test. Sensitive for FAI and anterosuperior labral pathology, but poorly specific.
  • FABER / Patrick’s (flexion, abduction, external rotation) — pain in the groin suggests the hip; pain in the buttock suggests the sacroiliac joint.
  • Thomas test — hip flexor contracture; note whether the restriction is in iliopsoas (hip stays flexed) or rectus femoris (knee extends).
  • Trendelenburg / single-leg stance — abductor function.
  • Log roll — passive rotation with the leg relaxed; the most specific test for intra-articular pathology, because it moves only the joint and nothing else.

rows: Supine, probe along the femoral neck axis (oblique sagittal)
The window for effusion — measure the anterior capsule-to-bone distance. >7 mm, or >1–2 mm more than the other side, indicates an effusion. Also the intra-articular injection target
Transverse at the level of the iliopectineal eminence
Tendon, bursa, and dynamic assessment for internal snapping
Lateral, transverse then longitudinal over each facet
Gluteus medius on the lateral facet, minimus on the anterior facet; tendinopathy, tears, bursal fluid
Hamstring origin, ischiogluteal bursa; the sciatic nerve lies just lateral — identify it before injecting
Transverse, just medial and inferior to the ASIS
A small oval nerve between the fascia lata and iliaca; the target for diagnostic block in meralgia paraesthetica
Always image-guided — ultrasound or fluoroscopy. Anterolateral or lateral approach to the femoral head–neck junction
The joint is deep and the femoral neurovascular bundle lies anteromedially. Blind injection is unacceptable here — unlike the knee or shoulder
Ultrasound-guided, from lateral to medial at the iliopectineal eminence
Keeps the needle away from the femoral vessels and nerve
Lateral, ultrasound-guided to the bursa superficial to the gluteal tendons
Avoid injecting into the tendon. Consider whether a load programme is the better first-line option
Ultrasound-guided just medial to the ASIS
Diagnostic and therapeutic in meralgia paraesthetica

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
A hot, painful hip held in flexion, abduction and external rotation is a septic hip until proven otherwise. That is the position of maximum capsular volume, and the patient adopts it to reduce intra-articular pressure. Aspirate under image guidance before any steroid.

In a child, the same picture demands urgent differentiation of septic arthritis from transient synovitis, using the Kocher criteria (non-weight-bearing, fever >38.5°C, ESR >40, WBC >12,000).
7.4 Common problems mapped back to anatomy

rows: Groin pain referred to the knee via the obturator nerve; internal rotation lost first
Abnormal contact in flexion–internal rotation → anterosuperior labral and chondral damage; positive FADIR
Loss of the suction seal; catching, clicking, deep groin pain
Undercoverage → rim overload → labral hypertrophy then failure → early arthritis
Vessels run along the neck → disrupted by displaced fracture or dislocation
Compression by the ITB in adduction → avoid crossing legs, side-lying, ITB stretching
Reproducible clunk moving from FABER to extension
Sciatic nerve in the subgluteal space
A diagnosis of exclusion — rule out lumbar radiculopathy first
Obturator nerve referral. Examine and image the hip
Increase in articular surface / volume provided by the labrum
Joint reaction force in single-leg stance
Reduction in joint reaction force from a contralateral cane
Anterior capsule-to-bone distance on ultrasound indicating an effusion
Proportion in whom the undivided sciatic nerve passes below piriformis
AVN risk after a displaced intracapsular neck fracture

content_config.body:
• The hip is stable by design — disease presents as stiffness and pain, not instability.
  • Internal rotation is lost first. Full painless internal rotation makes significant hip joint disease unlikely.
  • The functional deficit patients notice is reaching the foot — socks, shoes, toenails. Ask about it directly.
  • The abductor lever arm is a third of the body-weight lever arm, so the joint sees 2.5–3 × body weight in single-leg stance.
  • A cane in the CONTRALATERAL hand cuts joint load by about a third. Ipsilateral achieves almost nothing.
  • All three capsular ligaments tighten in extension — which is why we stand on the iliofemoral ligament and dislocate in flexion.
  • The position of comfort is 30° flexion, 30° abduction, slight external rotation — maximum capsular volume, and the posture of a septic hip.
  • The labrum’s suction seal matters more than the tear — lose the seal and cartilage load rises.
  • The capsule attaches at the intertrochanteric line anteriorly, so intracapsular fractures threaten the head’s blood supply and extracapsular ones do not.
  • Retinacular branches of the MFCA run along the neck — the anatomy behind every case of post-traumatic AVN.
  • Trendelenburg is named for the weak side; the opposite side drops. The lurch is compensation, not pain behaviour.
  • Psoas is innervated directly from L1–L3, iliacus by the femoral nerve — hip flexion may be preserved in a femoral nerve lesion.
  • Lateral hip pain is gluteal tendinopathy, not bursitis, and it is driven by compression in adduction.
  • Hip pathology refers to the knee via the obturator nerve. A child with knee pain and a normal knee has a hip problem until proven otherwise.
  • Never inject the hip blind. It is deep, and the femoral neurovascular bundle lies anteromedially.

• Hot, painful hip held in flexion–abduction–external rotation, refusing weight-bearing → septic arthritis. Aspirate under guidance before any steroid.
  • Groin pain and inability to weight-bear after a fall, with a normal radiograph → occult femoral neck fracture. Plain films miss up to 10%; get MRI or CT.
  • Insidious groin pain in a runner, military recruit, or athlete with low energy availability → femoral neck stress fracture. A tension-sided (superolateral) fracture can complete and displace — stop loading and image urgently.
  • Adolescent with knee or thigh pain, an antalgic gait and loss of internal rotation → SCFE. Examine the hip; obligatory external rotation on flexion is the classic sign.
  • Hip pain in a patient on corticosteroids, with alcohol dependence, or sickle cell disease → AVN. Radiographs are normal early; MRI is the investigation.
  • Night pain, rest pain, weight loss, or a history of malignancy → image. The proximal femur is a common site of metastasis, and a lytic lesion risks a pathological fracture.
  • Progressive weakness with a Trendelenburg gait and no hip pain → think neurological: L5 radiculopathy, superior gluteal lesion, or a myopathy.
Anatomy only. Hip biomechanics — gait kinetics, joint reaction force modelling and the mechanics of arthroplasty — is treated separately.
